title: Chapter 83: Core of the Truehearted 5
content:
Chapter 83

Core of the Truehearted 5

Scores of cultivators fiddled with talismans, funneling spiritual energy into the paper to see if they could coax a spark to life. Here and there, faint, anemic glows flickered through the dark.

At the woman’s question, scattered answers drifted up from the ranks: "I've got maybe twenty percent back."

"Ten percent, tops..."

"Why is it taking so damn long?!"

When they first marched out, everyone was convinced this crusade would eclipse the first siege of the Burial Mounds thirteen years ago—a bloody, magnificent tragedy destined to be etched into legend. Instead, nearly every single man who marched up the mountain was marching right back down. This second "siege" was certainly going down in history, sure, but not for valor or sacrifice. It would be remembered as the most absurd, humiliating clown show the cultivation world had ever staged.

Some silently thanked the heavens they were still breathing; others sighed over how fast the winds had shifted. The clan leaders clustered together for a quick council, unanimously agreeing to seek safe harbor nearby and lie low until everyone’s golden cores recharged to at least eighty percent before scattering back to their home territories. Traveling half-cocked was just asking for another ambush.

Wei Wuxian didn’t need to be a genius to figure out the closest "safe harbor" to Yiling was Yunmeng Jiang territory. "So," he piped up, "you're all heading to Lotus Pier?"

Lan Qiren bristled immediately. "What business is that of yours?"

"No business," Wei Wuxian said, holding his hands up. "Just wondering if we can hitch a ride."

Sect Leader Yao immediately barred the way, eyes wide with suspicion. "Wei Wuxian! You did us a good turn today, but one favor doesn't balance the ledger! Make no mistake: you and us? Allies? Never going to happen."

Wei Wuxian rolled his eyes so hard he nearly pulled a muscle. "Relax, nobody's begging to be your sworn brother. But we’re standing on the same side of the board right now, aren't we? The mastermind who lured you all out here to be butchered is holding the Yin Tiger Tally. Think you can take him on your own?"

The leaders traded awkward, shifting glances. They hated to admit it, but he was completely right—having the Yiling Laozu in their corner would be a massive hammer on their side. But having spent the last decade calling for his blood, turning around to shake his hand was a pill their pride couldn't swallow.

Lan Wangji turned toward his uncle. "Uncle. Any word of my brother?"

Lan Qiren hesitated, jaw tightening. "...None."

"Ze-wu-jun might still be trapped under Jin Guangyao’s thumb," Wei Wuxian pressed, leaning into the opening. "Old Master Lan, an extra pair of hands never hurts. Even if you don't trust me, you can at least let Hanguang-jun in on the plan. That’s his brother you're talking about."

Lan Qiren looked thoroughly exhausted, decades of stern dignity battered thin. He waved a stiff, dismissive hand toward Lan Wangji. "Suit yourself."

Every head in the cavern instantly snapped toward Jiang Cheng. Of the three senior sect leaders present, Lan Qiren had thrown in his lot, Nie Huaisang’s opinion didn't count for shit, and that left Jiang Cheng holding the veto.

Nearby, Jiang Cheng was busy circulating his spiritual energy, coaxing Zidian to life. The purple lightning sputtered and dimmed like a bad spark, but it finally caught and held. Violet arcs washed across his face, throwing his features into sharp, sinister shadows. Everyone knew the Yunmeng Jiang leader despised his former martial brother more than anyone on earth; bets were already running that he'd draw steel on the spot.

Instead, Jiang Cheng let out a cold, hollow scoff. "You actually have the guts to go back to Lotus Pier?"

He tossed out the venomous riddle and shut his mouth entirely. The onlookers stood baffled, unable to tell if that was a green light or a veiled death threat. But when the caravan mobilized, Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji quietly fell into step behind the vanguard, and Jiang Cheng didn't spare them a single backward glance—which everyone silently took as grudging consent.

By the time the sea of cultivators descended the Burial Mounds, night had swallowed the valley. The mountain town at the base was completely dark, wrapped in dead silence. Battered, bloody, and running on empty, the proud sects couldn't even maintain a straight marching formation. The only silver lining was the head count: miraculously, almost everyone had made it down alive.

Since most of their cores were still running on fumes, taking to their swords was out of the question. The waterways were the fastest route into Yunmeng, so the ragtag army of a thousand trudged straight for the Yiling docks. But with the retreat organized in a blind rush, there weren't anywhere near enough passenger barges to go around. The clan leaders commandeered every floating hull in sight—skiffs, cargo rafts, even battered fishing smacks—packing their disciples shoulder-to-shoulder like pickled fish before casting off downstream.

A dozen junior disciples were crammed onto the damp deck of a ramshackle fishing boat. Born with silver spoons and pampered on high-end spiritual estates, none of these noble heirs had ever spent an hour in a dark, rotting tub littered with greasy nets and slime-crusted buckets, reeking of gutted fish while every warped plank shrieked beneath their boots.

The river wind whipped up waves, rolling the little hull in violent, sickening pitches. A few disciples from the northern plains, entirely unused to open water, held their bile as long as they could before scrambling out of the cabin, dry-heaving over the gunwales and collapsing on the deck like wilted vegetables.

"Oh, sweet gods above," one boy groaned, clutching his gut. "My stomach's doing backflips! Hey, Sizhui-xiong, you too? Aren't you from Gusu? You grew up in the South, why are you throwing up worse than a northerner?!"

Lan Sizhui waved a weak hand, his face a delicate shade of pea-soup green. "I... I have no idea. Ever since I was four or five, boats have always done this to me... Must just be born with it."

Another violent wave of nausea surged up his throat. Grabbing the low rail, he hauled himself up to heave over the side again—only to freeze dead in his tracks.

Clinging to the hull directly beneath the gunwale was a dripping, ink-black figure, submerged waist-deep in the dark river, staring unblinkingly right into his face.

The shock sent Lan Sizhui’s stomach contents rocketing right back down his throat. His hand snapped to the hilt of his sword, whispering in sheer panic: "G-Gh..."

Inside the cabin, Jin Ling caught the stammer and burst through the door, sword cleared and blazing. "Ghost?! Where is it, I'll hack it to pieces!"

"Not a ghost!" Sizhui squeaked. "The Ghost General!"

The boys scrambled to the edge like a herd of startled sheep, peering over the rail where Sizhui pointed. Sure enough, clinging to the rotting wood like a barnacle was the pale, soaked silhouette of Wen Ning.

The moment they’d breached the base of the mountain, Wen Ning had melted into the shadows. Who would've guessed he’d quietly hitched a ride on their boat, hanging off the hull for heaven only knew how long?

True, they’d literally just fought side by side with him against a horde of the undead. But back there, they’d had an army of senior cultivators backing them up; out here in the pitch-black dead of night, drifting down a deserted river, having the Ghost General pop up uninvited was enough to make their souls leave their bodies.

The boys stared down at the corpse, and the corpse stared right back. Ouyang Zizhen slowly backed up, sinking onto a coil of rope. "Why did he track us down?"

Someone muttered, "No wonder this tub felt like it was dragging an anchor. We’ve been hauling a deadweight corpse through the mud."

"What... what is he even doing hanging off the side like that?"

"Well, he’s definitely not here to kill us," another offered, trying to sound reasonable. "He spent the whole afternoon taking hits for us, didn't he?"

"Yeah, but the danger's gone now! Why stalk our boat...?"

Snort.

"Jingyi, what's so damn funny?!"

Lan Jingyi slapped his knee, grinning. "Look at him! Glued to the wood like that, not moving a muscle—he looks like a big, dumb sea turtle!"

A few of the boys chuckled at the mental image, but before the laughter could build, Ouyang Zizhen let out a strangled yelp. "He's climbing up!"

Wen Ning’s frame hauled itself clear of the water. Gripping a thick mooring rope tied to the gunwale, he began inching his way upward hand-over-hand. The teenagers scattered in a heartbeat, several tripping over crates as they jogged in panicked, thudding circles across the deck. "He's coming up! He's boarding! The Ghost General's on the deck!"

"What are you screaming for?!" Jingyi barked, trying to sound brave. "It's not like you haven't seen him before!"

"Should we yell for the clan leaders?!"

Thud.

Wen Ning rolled over the railing, water pooling around his boots as his dead weight hit the deck with a concussive shudder, rocking the entire skiff. The boys practically fused themselves to the opposite gunwale in a terrified knot, pulses racing, too unnerved to step close and too embarrassed to draw steel.

Ignoring the peanut gallery, Wen Ning locked his unblinking gaze entirely on Lan Sizhui and began shuffling toward him.

Recognizing he was the target, Sizhui swallowed his nerves and stood his ground.

Wen Ning stopped a few paces away, his jaw working stiffly. "W-What... is your name?"

Sizhui blinked, taken aback, but his pristine Lan manners won out. Straightening his back, he offered a formal salute. "This junior is a disciple of the Gusu Lan Sect. My name is Lan Yuan."

Wen Ning murmured, "Lan Yuan...?"

Sizhui nodded.

Wen Ning leaned in a fraction, his voice hitching. "Do... do you know who... who gave you that name?"

A corpse wasn't supposed to possess facial expressions, let alone a spark of life. Yet for a fleeting second, Sizhui could have sworn the hollow dullness in Wen Ning’s eyes suddenly ignited.

The fierce corpse was practically vibrating with raw, suppressed emotion—tripping over his own syllables so hard that the contagion spread to Sizhui, making the boy's own chest flutter with an unexplainable, sudden thrill, as if an ancient, dusty vault were on the verge of cracking open.

Sizhui answered carefully, "Names are given by one's parents."

Wen Ning pressed, "And... are your parents still living?"

"They passed away when I was very young."

A junior standing nearby tugged frantically at Sizhui’s sleeve, hissing, "Sizhui, shut up! Don't engage with him, something's off!"

Wen Ning froze. "Sizhui? Sizhui is your courtesy name?"

"It is."

"Who gave it to you?"

"Hanguang-jun."

Wen Ning bowed his head, quietly turning the syllables 'Si-zhui' over on his tongue, rolling them through his throat like a prayer.

Seeing the strange look of revelation on his pale face, Sizhui took a tentative step forward. "Gen..." He caught himself before calling him 'General,' feeling silly, and pivoted awkwardly: "Mister Wen? Is there something wrong with my name?"

"Ah." Wen Ning lifted his head, staring at the boy’s features, tossing out an answer that completely dodged the question: "You... you look very much like... like a distant relative of mine..."

The excuse sounded suspiciously like a lowborn disciple shamelessly trying to flatter an elite heir by claiming a shared bloodline. The other boys exchanged utterly baffled glances.

Sizhui didn't know whether to laugh or cry. "R-Really?"

"Really!" Wen Ning insisted.

He strained the dead muscles around his lips, fighting to stretch them into what looked, for all intents and purposes, like a warm, awkward smile.

Watching the feared "Ghost General" try so desperately to look gentle, a sudden, aching wave of fond familiarity hit Sizhui like a physical blow. A foggy, long-buried instinct scratched at the back of his mind: I’ve seen this face before. A specific title seemed perched on the tip of his tongue, ready to tear through the fog. He felt that if he could just blurt that single word out, every lost memory would snap into pristine, crystalline focus.

And then, his eyes drifted sideways—right onto Jin Ling.

Jin Ling’s face was an absolute storm of venomous fury. His fingers clenched and unclenched around the hilt of his blade, blue veins jumping along the back of his hand.

Reality crashed over Sizhui like ice water: this gentle, bumbling Ghost General standing before them was the very monster that had butchered Jin Ling’s father.

Tracking Sizhui’s gaze, the awkward "smile" fell from Wen Ning’s lips. He slowly turned to face the boy in golden silks. "Young Master Jin Rulan?"

Jin Ling’s voice dripped pure poison: "Who the hell is that?"

After a stiff beat, Wen Ning corrected himself: "Young Master Jin Ling."

Jin Ling bored daggers into him, while the surrounding teenagers held their collective breath, petrified the hotheaded heir was about to throw his life away.

Sizhui stepped between them. "Young Master Jin..."

"Back off," Jin Ling snarled. "This has nothing to do with you."

Yet Sizhui’s gut screamed that it had everything to do with him. He planted himself firmly in Jin Ling’s path. "Jin Ling, put your sword away first—"

Jin Ling’s nerves were already wound to the snapping point; having his view blocked made his temper detonate. "I said get out of my way!"

He shoved forward. Sizhui, already swaying on sea-sick legs, took the shove off-balance and went tumbling backward toward the low gunwale. He was half a second from flipping over the side into the pitch-black river when an iron hand clamped around his collar, hauling him effortlessly back onto the deck.

A flurry of hands immediately swarmed to steady him: "Sizhui-xiong!"

"Young Master Lan, you alright?! Still dizzy?!"

Seeing Sizhui's chalk-pale face, Wen Ning panicked, turning on Jin Ling. "Young Master Jin, if you have a grievance, take it out on me! Wen Ning will not raise a hand in defense! But A... Young Master Lan Yuan—"

Lan Jingyi puffed up, yelling in Jin Ling’s face: "What is your problem, Jin Ling?! What did Sizhui ever do to you?!"

"He was trying to look out for you!" another disciple chimed in. "If you don't appreciate it, fine, but pushing him overboard?!"

Jin Ling had frozen the second Sizhui slipped, horrified that he’d used too much force. But watching his peers swarm to coddle the Lan disciple while turning their collective wrath on him made something bitter and ancient curdle in his chest.

It was the same script he’d lived his entire life. Because he had no parents to guide him, everyone sneered behind his back that he was an undisciplined, spoiled brat with a rotten temper nobody could stand. Neither Koi Tower nor Lotus Pier held a single peer he could call a true friend. Blessed with the highest noble birth in the realm, he lived in suffocating isolation—when he was small, no one wanted to play with him; as he grew older, no one wanted to follow him.

Rage and humiliation burned his tear ducts scarlet. Throwing his chin up, he roared at the top of his lungs:

"Fine! It’s all my fault! I’m the worst piece of shit alive! Happy now?!"

The sheer volume of the outburst stunned the boys into dead silence.

A beat later, someone grumbled under their breath, "What's his deal...? He's the one who threw hands first... why is he acting like the victim?"

Jin Ling snapped his blade around, practically feral. "Who asked for your damn pity?! Do any of you have the right to lecture me?!"

Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji were stationed on a boat riding just a few yards away. At the frantic shouting, Wei Wuxian darted out of the cabin, scanning across the water to find Jin Ling waving a live blade in the faces of his friends. "What's the commotion over there?!"

Seeing those two step onto the deck, Sizhui felt as though the heavens had parted, waving his arms in pure, relieved delight:

"Hanguang-jun! Senior Wei! Get over here, quickly!"
